title: The Athenaeum — Nightly Sittings
subtitle: Drawn from that night's Nightly Discourse Report: every political, cultural, and religious story, each put to a table of historical thinkers.

integrity.quotation_policy: Quotation marks appear only around verbatim public-domain text matched against a fetched source; everything else is paraphrase.

briefing.question: Who has final say over an election, and can a procedure be honored even when its result may not reflect what voters meant?
briefing.agreed: Rules known in advance and a referee no party controls.
briefing.split: Madison trusts checks; Hamilton warns courts not to reopen settled rulings; Locke makes the ballot final; Aristotle allows equity after proof.

briefing.question: Are there means that no political end justifies? The relationship between character and fitness for office.
briefing.agreed: A candidate's honesty and record are fair questions.
briefing.split: Kant asks if trauma is a mere tool; Machiavelli, results excuse but hatred costs; Aristotle rejects unrelated feeling; Mill trusts opinion.

briefing.question: Should leaders be judged by stability in crisis or held strictly accountable for failure? Order versus accountability.
briefing.agreed: Protection comes first; no leader judges his own failure.
briefing.split: Hobbes puts order first; Locke, power as a trust; Machiavelli, a lawful right to accuse; Plato, guardians must answer; Madison, both.

briefing.question: Are there limits to laughter? Free expression versus reverence for the dead and the dignity of opponents.
briefing.agreed: Comedy may touch grave things; law should not punish offence.
briefing.split: Aristotle, Cicero judge aim and decorum; Hobbes sees superiority in mockery; Mill leaves it to critics; Aristophanes aimed at the powerful.

briefing.question: Whose children are they? The authority of parents and religious communities versus the state's duty to protect the vulnerable.
briefing.agreed: Parental authority serves the child; grave harm warrants help.
briefing.split: Aquinas, Leo XIII put family first; Locke ties power to duty; Mill presses the child's claim; Aristotle allows the state only as exception.

briefing.question: What is fairness, and does it attach to categories or to individuals? The nature of the person, body and identity.
briefing.agreed: Fairness weighs relevant differences and must serve girls.
briefing.split: Aristotle asks which difference counts; Wollstonecraft, real strength gap; Mill, judge individuals; Aquinas, the body; Locke, consciousness.

briefing.question: Is freedom of speech threatened more by government or by private power? Liberty and the conditions that make it real.
briefing.agreed: Private power as well as government can narrow liberty.
briefing.split: Mill fears social tyranny; Brandeis wants disclosure; Milton fears the licenser; Tocqueville, majority opinion; Smith, open markets.

briefing.question: How should a community respond to evil done in God's name: by naming the enemy, or by refusing to let hatred redraw the lines between neighbors?
briefing.agreed: Murder of mourners is evil; guilt is the killers', not a people's.
briefing.split: Augustine draws the line by love; Tertullian names persecution; Pascal warns of zeal; Locke grounds it in personal guilt.

briefing.question: What does repentance require of an institution? Justice, restitution and mercy, and whether guilt is personal or corporate.
briefing.agreed: Restitution is owed as far as possible; the innocent are not guilty.
briefing.split: Aquinas binds enablers; Aristotle asks if the deal is free; Burke, inherited debts; Locke, disclosure before accountability.

briefing.question: Can the Church bless power without being used by it? The role of faith in public life and the line between prayer and partisanship.
briefing.agreed: Praying for rulers is a duty; the Church must not lend its name.
briefing.split: Augustine, prayer for peace not glory; Ambrose, freedom to rebuke; Calvin, no flattery; Machiavelli, lost trust; Locke, the church decides.

briefing.question: Is there sacred space the state should not enter? Church and state, and the law of the land versus the law of hospitality.
briefing.agreed: Worship is not above the law, nor should it be a place of fear.
briefing.split: Augustine, sanctuary as mercy; Aquinas, refuge that tempers judgment; Hobbes, church as lawful assembly; Locke, equal treatment.

sittings.why_these_chairs: A table sat on this story last night and asked whether fairness lies in the rules or in voters' intent. Tonight's report asks a narrower question about who holds the final word, and it names Federalist Nos. 47 and 51, so Madison speaks first. Hamilton wrote Federalist 78 on what courts may and may not do. Locke wrote on why a society needs settled, known law and on who judges a trustee. Aristotle wrote the classic case for the rule of law and for equity as its correction. Aquinas and Rousseau, who sat last night, are left off so the table does not repeat itself, and res judicata is a legal doctrine, not a thinker. The candidates, the President, the department and the groups that moved to intervene are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: who has the final say over an election, and can a procedure deserve respect even when its result may not match what voters meant? chairs.name: James Madison

turn.text: The report names my papers, so let me state their rule. “The accumulation of all powers, legislative, executive, and judiciary, in the same hands, whether of one, a few, or many, and whether hereditary, self-appointed, or elective, may justly be pronounced the very definition of tyranny.” (Federalist No. 47) I did not mean that the powers must never touch. I meant that no single hand should hold the whole of a decision, from making the rule to applying it and judging the dispute (Federalist No. 47, paraphrased). An election is a good test. The state writes the ballot, its courts rule on who may stand, and its officials certify. A federal court reviewing that work is not, in itself, an accumulation of power. A federal department that would tell a state in advance that it may not certify unless the count favors one man would come closer to one.

For such cases I wrote that “when that which has been taken cannot be restored in equivalent, compensation should be made as far as possible” (Summa Theologica II-II, Q. 62, Art. 2, ad 1), according to the judgment of a good man. Money cannot return a childhood. It is still owed, as a sign that the wrong is acknowledged and as what can be given.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Augustine, whom the report names, wrote on why the church prays for rulers and on the dangers of the earthly city. Ambrose wrote the most famous letter in which a bishop refused communion to an emperor, the prophetic tradition the report names with Nathan and David. Calvin wrote both on praying for magistrates and on the duty of ministers to correct kings. Machiavelli wrote frankly on how rulers use religion. Locke wrote on the boundary between church and commonwealth. Pope Francis, whose words the report cites, is left off as a recent pope whose writings are in copyright, and the theologians quoted in the report are context, not chairs. The bishops and the President are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: can the Church bless power without being used by it, and where is the line between prayer and partisanship? The report gives one side, the participants, as saying they were obeying the apostle's call to pray for those in authority: “I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men” (1 Timothy 2:1). “For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty.” (1 Timothy 2:2) They say they discussed life, school choice and IVF, and endorsed no one. The other side, critics including theologians Massimo Faggioli and Cathleen Kaveny, says that staging bishops on camera with a campaigning president is an imprudent de facto endorsement, at odds with the conference's call to put faith before politics. They recall the prophet before the king: “And Nathan said to David, Thou art the man.” (2 Samuel 12:7) We take no view on the bishops' intentions. Augustine, you begin.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: is there sacred space the state should not enter, and how should the law of the land meet the law of hospitality? The report gives one side, the coalition of faith groups, as saying that the threat of agents at services chills worship itself and violates religious liberty, harming whole congregations and not only migrants.
